sections.heading: Own the data center or rent the cloud?
bullets: An AI lab's make-or-buy question: renting cloud GPUs means paying a landlord's margin and competing for scarce allocation, but zero construction risk; owning means carrying capital, construction, and operations in exchange for control, cost, and speed at scale

The math turns on utilization and duration: for bursty or uncertain needs, renting wins easily; for a lab that will saturate hundreds of megawatts for years, the landlord's markup compounds into billions — the scale where owning starts to pay

Vertical integration buys freedom from other people's queues: a self-builder chooses its own sites, power strategy, hardware mix, and construction pace — no negotiating for allocation, no waiting behind another tenant's expansion

The price is concentrated risk: an owner carries the depreciation, the permits, the community relations, and the technology-obsolescence exposure that a renter quietly passes to its landlord — vertical integration converts a flexible expense into an illiquid bet

sections.heading: Compressing the build: how months become days
bullets: Conventional data-center delivery is sequential — design, permit, build, energize, commission, each waiting on the last; radical compression comes from running those phases in parallel and knowingly accepting the rework risk that sequencing exists to avoid

A brownfield shell is the biggest single shortcut: an abandoned factory already has structure, zoning, water, and road access — reusing it deletes a year of sitework and turns the project into an interior fit-out at industrial scale

Temporary infrastructure bridges every remaining gap: mobile generation while permanent power is permitted and built, rented cooling while chillers ship — the philosophy that a working cluster now plus retrofit later beats a perfect cluster in two years

Decision latency is the hidden schedule item: a single owner-operator who approves changes in hours removes the approval loops — owner, engineer, contractor, financier — that consume weeks on conventional projects; organizational structure is itself a construction technology

sections.heading: Air permits: the law of what comes out of the stack
bullets: US air law starts with the National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS) — federal limits on pollutant concentrations in outdoor air, including ozone, fine particulates, and nitrogen oxides — and regulates each combustion source by how much it adds to local air

Size thresholds decide the process: a 'major source' triggers rigorous pre-construction review with modeling, public comment, and best-available-control requirements; staying below thresholds — or claiming temporary status — permits far faster with far less scrutiny

Nitrogen oxides (NOx) are the data-center-relevant pollutant: gas turbines produce them, they drive ozone formation in already-burdened neighborhoods, and selective catalytic reduction (SCR — injecting ammonia across a catalyst in the exhaust) is the standard control

The live legal frontier is aggregation and duration: whether dozens of nominally mobile turbines operating together for months constitute one major stationary source is exactly the kind of question that lands in federal court — and its answer prices speed for every builder

sections.heading: Real-time data: training on the present tense
bullets: Standard training corpora are snapshots — web scrapes months old — so models arrive slightly frozen in the past; a live platform generates data about events as they unfold, a structurally different feed from any archive

Freshness matters most where the world changes fastest: news, markets, culture, and live conversation — a model with training or retrieval access to the present can answer questions that static-corpus rivals must decline or guess at

The flywheel: the platform produces data, the model trained on it powers features on the platform, the features drive usage, and usage produces more data — a loop where owning the venue and owning the model reinforce each other

The caveats are structural: platform text is noisy, adversarial (spam, bots, manipulation), and demographically skewed — refining a live feed into training-grade data is its own engineering discipline, and exclusive access invites both competitive and regulatory scrutiny

sections.heading: Grid power vs your own power plant
bullets: A single-tenant AI campus faces a choice the grid never used to pose: wait years for a utility connection delivering cheap, reliable, professionally maintained power — or generate on-site starting in months, at higher cost per megawatt-hour, with the operational burden in-house

The decision inputs: time-to-power, delivered cost per megawatt-hour, emissions and permitting exposure, and reliability engineering — the grid wins three of the four and loses the one an arms-race participant weighs most heavily

Batteries change the on-site equation: a large battery buffer absorbs the violent load swings of synchronized GPU training (which generators alone handle poorly), rides through generator trips, and lets an islanded campus run with grid-class stability entirely off-grid

The end-state is usually hybrid: on-site generation carries the campus while the interconnection matures, then the grid becomes primary with on-site as supplement — the sequencing, not the choice of technologies, is the actual strategic decision

sections.heading: How big is that cluster, really?
bullets: GPU count is the headline metric and the least comparable: chip generations differ several-fold in per-unit performance, so '200,000 GPUs' of mixed vintages says little — hence 'H100-equivalents,' restating a whole fleet in units of one reference chip

FLOPS (floating-point operations per second) measure theoretical arithmetic peak — but the figure depends on the precision format quoted and on whether the workload can actually keep the math units fed, so published FLOPS are ceilings, not throughput

Megawatts are the honest common denominator: power draw is physically measurable, vintage-agnostic, and hard to inflate — which is why operators, utilities, and analysts increasingly denominate AI capacity in megawatts and gigawatts rather than chips

'Coherent cluster' is the qualifier that matters for training: gigawatts scattered across disconnected sites cannot train one frontier model — what counts is capacity linked into a single fast fabric, one enormous machine rather than many medium ones

flashcards.q: When does owning a data center beat renting cloud GPUs?
flashcards.a: When utilization and duration are both high: a lab that will saturate hundreds of megawatts for years watches the landlord's markup compound into billions, so owning pays. For bursty or uncertain demand, renting wins — the cloud's premium is the price of flexibility and someone else's construction risk.

flashcards.q: What risks does a self-building AI lab take on that a cloud renter avoids?
flashcards.a: Depreciation on rapidly obsoleting hardware, construction and permitting exposure, community relations, and the operations burden of running power and cooling. Renting passes all of that to a landlord; owning converts a flexible operating expense into a concentrated, illiquid bet.

flashcards.q: How does parallelizing design, permitting, and construction compress a build schedule?
flashcards.a: Conventional sequencing makes each phase wait for the last specifically to avoid rework. Running them concurrently overlaps months of waiting — at the accepted risk that a late design or permit change forces tearing out finished work. It's a deliberate trade of money and risk for time.

flashcards.q: Why is an abandoned factory such a valuable starting point for an AI campus?
flashcards.a: The structure, industrial zoning, water, and road access already exist — deleting roughly a year of sitework and approvals. The project becomes an interior fit-out at industrial scale rather than greenfield construction, which is how record-speed cluster builds start ahead before day one.

The National Ambient Air Quality Standards: federal limits on the concentration of pollutants — ozone, fine particulates, nitrogen oxides, and others — in outdoor air. Every combustion source is regulated by how much it contributes to local air relative to these limits.

flashcards.q: Why does 'major source' status matter so much in air permitting?
flashcards.a: Crossing the major-source threshold triggers rigorous pre-construction review — air modeling, public comment, best-available-control technology. Below the threshold, or under temporary-equipment status, permitting is dramatically faster with less scrutiny. The classification, not the technology, often sets the project schedule.

The standard control for nitrogen oxides from gas turbines: ammonia is injected into the exhaust stream across a catalyst, converting NOx into nitrogen and water. NOx matters because it drives ozone formation — the pollutant fights over data-center gas fleets are mostly NOx fights.

flashcards.q: What legal question do fleets of 'mobile' gas turbines raise?
flashcards.a: Aggregation and duration: whether dozens of nominally temporary units operating together for months add up to a single major stationary source requiring full permits. The answer — being tested in federal court — effectively prices how much schedule advantage temporary-equipment status can legally buy.

flashcards.q: What makes real-time platform data different from standard training corpora?
flashcards.a: Web-scrape corpora are months-old snapshots, so models arrive frozen slightly in the past. A live platform feeds events as they unfold — most valuable for news, markets, and culture. The costs: platform text is noisy, adversarial, and skewed, so refining it into training-grade data is real engineering.

flashcards.q: Why do batteries make an off-grid AI campus viable?
flashcards.a: Synchronized GPU training swings load violently in milliseconds — generators alone respond too slowly and trip. A large battery buffer absorbs the swings, rides through generator failures, and gives an islanded campus grid-class stability. Storage is the component that turns a generator farm into a power system.

flashcards.q: What is an 'H100-equivalent' and why do analysts use it?
flashcards.a: A fleet restated in units of one reference chip's performance, because raw GPU counts across mixed generations aren't comparable — vintages differ several-fold per unit. It's an imperfect normalization, but it lets a fleet of H100s, H200s, and newer racks be described as one number.

flashcards.q: Why are megawatts becoming the standard measure of AI cluster scale — with what caveat?
flashcards.a: Power draw is physically measurable, vintage-agnostic, and hard to inflate, unlike chip counts or theoretical FLOPS. The caveat is coherence: gigawatts scattered across disconnected sites can't train one frontier model — only capacity linked into a single fast fabric counts as one machine.
